name: Neutral-Atiouandaronk
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Neutral Huron language' (rev. 2026-06-07), citing Mithun 1979, Thwaites, Hanzeli 1969, Julian 2010.
sources.note: Nothing; tertiary summary: two proper names preserved, Jesuit grammar/dictionary lost, Mithun (1979:160) cites Roy Wright's note that Neutral lacked the sound changes distinguishing Wendat.

sources.citation: Julian, Charles. 2010. A history of the Iroquoian languages. PhD thesis, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg. 595 pp. Section 18.5 'Neutral', pp. 338-339.
sources.note: Nothing. p. 339: 'Two words of what may represent authentic Neutral are preserved in a letter sent to France in 1627 by Jesuit Father Joseph de la Roche Dallion.. the name of a town, <Ounontisaston>, and its chief, <Souharissen> (Le Clercq 1882: 265, 269). From these words.. one can discern that Neutral was indeed an Iroquoian language, was rhotic.., had causative perfects in *{-oh}.., and realized the reflex of PNI */o/ as [u] rather than [o].' No mention of accent/stress.

sources.citation: Thwaites, Reuben G. (ed.). 1898. The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, vol. 21 (Quebec and Hurons, 1641-1642). Cleveland: Burrows Brothers. pp. 188-189, 228-231.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 188/189: 'dans vne Nation differente de langage, au moins en plusieurs choses' / 'into a Nation different in language, at least in many respects'; p. 230/231: the Fathers 'eurent le moyen d'ajuster le Dictionnaire, & les [Regles] de la langue Huronne, a celle de ces Peuples' / 'were able to harmonize the Dictionary and the Syntax of the Huron language with those of these Tribes' (the resulting Neutral dictionary/grammar is lost).

sources.citation: Le Clercq, Chrestien. 1881 [1691]. First Establishment of the Faith in New France, vol. 1, tr. John Gilmary Shea. New York. pp. 265, 269 (de la Roche Daillon's letter of 1627).
sources.note: Nothing; primary attestation of the two Neutral names 'Souharissen' (p. 265) and 'Ounontisaston' (p. 269) in the English translation of Daillon's letter.
